title: How Often Should You Invest? Weekly vs Monthly Investing
summary: Is it better to invest daily, weekly or monthly? No schedule guarantees a better result. Match it to your paycheck, check per-trade costs, then keep it going.
body_markdown:
Investor.gov defines dollar-cost averaging as investing equal portions at regular intervals regardless of market moves. With a fixed dollar amount, you buy more shares when the price is lower and fewer when it is higher. The main practical value is a rule that does not depend on guessing the next move.


It does not guarantee a profit, protect against a long decline, or turn an unsuitable investment into a suitable one. If you already hold a lump sum, spreading it out also means holding cash longer;[FINRA notes that opportunity cost](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/dollar-cost-averaging) when it weighs dollar-cost averaging against investing all at once, and says dollar-cost averaging often produces lower returns than a lump sum, especially over longer periods.


That trade-off only exists when the money is already sitting in your account. When contributions come out of each paycheck, there is no lump sum waiting. FINRA notes that the cash-drag argument does not apply to workplace plan contributions for that reason: the money is invested as it is earned.
